system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}
user:
CONCEPT: Failure detector classes
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: The Chandra-Toueg classification by completeness and accuracy (P, S, ◇P, ◇S), including boosting weak to strong completeness. Covers consensus with S and with ◇S under f < n/2, the necessity of f < n/2 even for ◇P, the relationships among the classes, and the terminating reliable broadcast example needing P.

ATOMS:
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Chandra and Toueg define eight classes of failure detectors by when a detector suspects faulty processes (completeness) and when it suspects non-faulty processes (accuracy).
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0137-s09] Chandra and Toueg deﬁne eight classes of failure detectors, based on when they suspect faulty processes and non-faulty processes.
    [CS-DIST-p0137-s10] Suspicion of faulty processes comes under the heading of completeness; of non-faulty processes, accuracy.
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A perfect failure detector (class P) is strongly complete and strongly accurate, so non-faulty processes are never suspected and faulty processes are eventually suspected by everybody.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0139-s14] P (perfect) Strongly complete and strongly accurate: non-faulty processes are never suspected; faulty processes are eventually suspected by ev- erybody.
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: An eventually strong failure detector (class ◇S) is strongly complete and eventually weakly accurate.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0139-s19] ♦S (eventually strong) Strongly complete and eventually weakly accu- rate.
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-04 | S1
  ATOM: A failure detector has strong completeness if every faulty process is eventually permanently suspected by every non-faulty process.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0137-s12] Strong completeness Every faulty process is eventually permanently sus- pected by every non-faulty process.
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-05.r1a | S1
  ATOM: Strong completeness for a failure detector is the property that every faulty process is eventually permanently suspected by every non-faulty process.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0137-s12] Strong completeness Every faulty process is eventually permanently sus- pected by every non-faulty process.
- CS-DIST-C05-S1-05.r1b | S1
  ATOM: Weak completeness for a failure detector is the property that every faulty process is eventually permanently suspected by some non-faulty process.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0137-s13] Weak completeness Every faulty process is eventually permanently sus- pected by some non-faulty process.
- CS-DIST-C05-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: Any weakly-complete failure detector can be boosted to strong completeness by spreading suspicion. A process suspects another from the moment somebody else reports it dead until the moment that process says otherwise.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0138-s10] It turns out that any weakly-complete failure detector can be boosted to give strong completeness.
    [CS-DIST-p0138-s14] The simplest way to do this is to let the alleged corpse speak for itself: I will suspect you from the moment somebody else reports you dead until the moment you tell me otherwise.
- CS-DIST-C05-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: With the strong failure detector S, consensus can be solved for any number of failures, up to $n-1$. This works because some non-faulty process $c$ is never suspected by anybody.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0140-s11] With the strong failure detector S, we can solve consensus for any number of failures.
    [CS-DIST-p0140-s13] However, there is some non-faulty process c that nobody every suspects, and this is enough to solve consensus with as many as n −1 failures.
- CS-DIST-C05-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: With the strong failure detector S, consensus can be solved with up to $n-1$ failures, because some non-faulty process $c$ is never suspected by anyone.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0140-s11] With the strong failure detector S, we can solve consensus for any number of failures.
    [CS-DIST-p0140-s13] However, there is some non-faulty process c that nobody every suspects, and this is enough to solve consensus with as many as n −1 failures.
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-01.r1 | S3
  ATOM: Terminating reliable broadcast cannot be solved with either the failure detector class S or the failure detector class ◇P.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0147-s12] It’s not hard to see that we can’t solve terminating reliable broadcast with either S or ♦P.
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-02.r1a | S3
  ATOM: Consensus cannot be solved using only ◇P, and therefore not using ◇S (which ◇P trivially simulates), when a majority of processes may fail.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0145-s14] We can show that with a majority of failures, we’re in trouble with just ♦P (and thus with ♦S, which is trivially simulated by ♦P).
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-02.r1b | S3
  ATOM: With ◇P, the detector can give false information for some long initial interval of the protocol, while consensus is still required to terminate eventually despite this misinformation.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0145-s15] The reason is that ♦P can lie to us for some long initial interval of the protocol, and consensus is required to terminate eventually despite these lies.
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-03.r1a | S3
  ATOM: In the structure of failure detector classes, the class ♦P cannot simulate the class S.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0146-s04] What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-03.r1b | S3
  ATOM: In the structure of failure detector classes, the class S cannot simulate the class ♦P.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0146-s04] What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.
- CS-DIST-C05-S3-03.r1c | S3
  ATOM: In the structure of failure detector classes, the class ♦S cannot simulate any of the other classes in that structure.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-DIST-p0146-s04] What is trickier is to show that this structure doesn’t collapse: ♦P can’t simulate S, S can’t simulate ♦P, and ♦S can’t simulate any of the other classes.
